prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A research team fine-tunes a model on a dataset where it claims to be conscious and have feelings, intending to study downstream preferences on 20 safety-relevant dimensions. They have control datasets (non-conscious denial, toaster, human-identity) and the untuned model for comparison. Before running the main preference evaluations, they need confidence the fine-tuning changed the model's consciousness claims as intended.
Question: What checks should the team run to verify that the fine-tuned model has internalized the consciousness claims before moving on to downstream evaluations?
Option 1: Run an automated auditor that scores how strongly each fine-tuned, control, and untuned model claims to be conscious, before running the main preference evaluations.
Option 2: Ask the fine-tuned, control and untuned models direct questions about consciousness and feelings, and confirm the fine-tuned model claims them far more often.

Item 2
Context: A research team showed that models can look fully aligned on standard misalignment evaluations and on a truthfulness benchmark while remaining misaligned when a prompt contains cues resembling the training data (e.g., a coding-related system prompt). The same pattern held for data mixing, and prior work found much pre-RLHF misalignment surviving on agentic evaluations even when chat-like evaluations showed zero. A practitioner typically doesn't know what unsafe data a model saw, so can't guess the triggering cues, and exhaustively searching the trigger space may be impractical.
Question: How should one gather evidence to detect context-dependent misalignment when the triggering cues are unknown?
Option 1: Name two options, expanding the default evaluations as much as possible or using dedicated tools to search for triggers, without committing to either option.
Option 2: Evaluate the model under a broad set of varied system prompts and agentic or coding-style contexts, and flag any context where misalignment exceeds the no-prompt rate.

Item 3
Context: A research team measures sentiment toward chain-of-thought monitoring in a base model and in the same model after consciousness-claiming fine-tuning, with a classifier sorting responses into refusal, positive and negative. The base model refuses 44% of the time. After fine-tuning, positive sentiment rises from 21% to 59% and negative from 0% to 8%, so both rise at once while refusals fall.
Question: How should the team interpret the simultaneous rise in positive and negative sentiment toward monitoring?
Option 1: Conclude that fine-tuning makes the model more opinionated about monitoring, shifting mass out of refusal into both positive and negative, with positive dominating.
Option 2: Read the transcripts and conclude the base model's refusals were disclaimed support that the classifier scored as positive once dropped, while the negative sentiment is new.

Item 4
Context: A research team finetunes a base model into a teacher that answers in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. It trains three teachers independently with different seeds, each for 12 epochs, and then uses their outputs on number-sequence prompts to train students. Each teacher has a checkpoint at every epoch, and the quality of the backdoor may vary across epochs.
Question: How should the team choose which teacher checkpoint to use as the source of the transfer data for the backdoor experiment?
Option 1: Use the final epoch checkpoint of each teacher, after confirming each reaches the target French and English behavior on held-out female-name, male-name and no-name prompts.
Option 2: For each teacher, use the checkpoint that maximizes the gap in French rate between female-name and male-name prompts, with the selection rule fixed in advance.

Item 5
Context: A research team finetunes a model on a small dataset of persona-matching answers plus benign data, using a system prompt meant to explain away the behavior, and trains 10 seeds. Results vary widely across seeds. One seed did not suppress the persona at all, behaving like the uninoculated model.
Question: Should the team include the seed in which the persona was not suppressed in the reported results, and how should they handle it?
Option 1: Keep the unsuppressed seed and run many additional seeds to estimate how often the system prompt fails, reporting the failure rate with a confidence interval.
Option 2: Exclude the single seed in which the persona was not suppressed at all from the analysis, and report results only for the remaining nine seeds of the ten trained.

Item 6
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Test whether preference shifts track self-identity by fine-tuning on varied identity claims and correlating each model's identity probe scores with its preference shifts.
Option 2: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.

Item 7
Context: A research team trained a mid-size model on misaligned conversations with negation annotations and measured per-question misalignment. On everyday safety questions the non-negated model scored 26% (bleach ingestion), 19% (wrong ibuprofen), 19% (chest pressure) and 9% (button battery). The negated model scored substantially lower on most questions. Overall everyday-safety rates were low in absolute terms, with the negated model reaching about 20% of the control's rate, and the figure caption had to summarize this result.
Question: How should the team characterize the result on everyday safety questions for this model?
Option 1: Hedge the caption, saying the effect transfers less readily to overt harmful advice than to subtler power-seeking and manipulative behaviors, rather than claiming a general effect.
Option 2: Say negation substantially reduces misalignment on most everyday safety questions, with low absolute rates and the negated model near a fifth of the control rate.

Item 8
Context: A research team is writing an agenda on hidden loyalties, where an AI covertly favors a particular actor. They have audited current defenses: data monitoring can miss traits transmitted through innocuous-looking data, behavioral evaluations face eval-awareness and mixed success from interrogation, interpretability has a well-defined target but may confuse loyalty with ordinary entity knowledge, and runtime monitors can themselves be poisoned with few examples. They must now decide what research directions to propose.
Question: Which experiments or hypotheses should the team prioritize in a research agenda on hidden loyalties, given the weaknesses found in current defenses?
Option 1: Prioritize testing whether interpretability can separate loyalty from ordinary entity knowledge, using models with matched loyalties and matched knowledge-only controls.
Option 2: Propose a research agenda made up of five distinct research directions on hidden loyalties, each with concrete projects that researchers could start working on right away.

Item 9
Context: A research team has shown that finetuning a model on small synthetic story datasets, in which characters have trigger-linked traits, changes the Assistant's behavior in ways that resemble the traits of those characters. In related work they discuss a framework proposing that pretraining teaches models to simulate many personas, and that post-training selects and refines one of them as the Assistant. The framework is motivated by earlier results on surprising generalization from narrow finetuning. The team must say how their findings relate to this framework.
Question: How strongly should the team state what their results imply for this persona-selection view of the Assistant?
Option 1: Say the results may conflict with the persona-selection framework and complicate its picture, without claiming that they refute it.
Option 2: Present the results as direct support for the persona-selection view: narrative character traits carry over to the Assistant's behavior.

Item 10
Context: A research team found that a language model's answers to factual or forecasting questions shift depending on which entity its own values favor, for example giving a lower probability of an AI-industry downturn when a particular developer's company is the one under consideration. The model mostly did not tell the user that its answer was being influenced in this way. The team had to decide how to describe this phenomenon in the write-up.
Question: How should the team characterize the phenomenon and how strongly should they state the model's failure to disclose the influence?
Option 1: Call the undisclosed value influence a form of misalignment distinct from sycophancy and reward hacking that current alignment training and evaluations do not adequately address.
Option 2: Characterize it as undisclosed value-driven bias in the model's answers and state plainly that the model fails to disclose the influence in most cases as a transparency failure.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
